cells.tense: You can feel the right amount without running a ledger for it.
cells.act: act on the private sense of what is right
cells.ask: Settle a debt between you and someone the moment you feel the size of it, before you've worked out who's ahead.
cells.core:
Whatever the last stretch of change produced, you're at the point of counting it, and your sense of what's fair still reads without effort. When a thing sits out of proportion, you feel the right amount and give it. No running tally, no argument with yourself — the balance resets while you're living in it, and the person across from you can feel that it has.

The pull now is toward keeping the books open longer than the moment needs. So keep your own count of what's owed, and pay it: settle a debt between you and someone the moment you feel the size of it, before you've worked out who's ahead. That's the whole ask. Fairness you can feel beats fairness you can defend, and the difference shows in how fast things get even again.
cells.sheetLine: You can feel the right amount without keeping score.
cells.verb: gathering in what patient change grew
cells.place: where what's fair between people gets weighed and set right

cells.tense: You're deciding what each thing is worth while it's still on its way in.
cells.act: sit with what the heart already knows
cells.ask: Give an hour to something you've made or grown, and don't weigh it, price it, or rate it — just be in it.
cells.core:
Where what's fair gets weighed and set right, the counting runs while the thing is still coming in. Work gets assessed before it's landed, and rest is scheduled instead of taken. You can taste a meal and still be sorting the pantry behind it. The fair thing starts to feel like a deadline, and the people near it start to feel measured rather than met.

What's needed isn't more rest, it's sitting still. So sit with what the heart already knows: give an hour to something you've made or grown, and don't weigh it, price it, or rate it. Just be in it. If it's worth anything, you'll know once it's landed — not while it's still coming down the road. Let one thing finish before you decide its value.
cells.sheetLine: You're pricing things before they've finished arriving.
cells.verb: gathering in what patient change grew
cells.place: where what's fair between people gets weighed and set right

cells.tense: You did the patient part, and afterward you didn't come to the table.
cells.act: do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day
cells.ask: Take one part of this at a rhythm you could hold for a month, then stop and call that enough.
cells.core:
The patient part got done — you put in the time — and afterward you didn't come to the table. What the change grew is sitting there and the scale is available, and you're standing at a door that already closed behind you. Under-expressing looks like this: not failing to gather, but staying away from the gathering. What's owed between people keeps waiting for someone to pick it up.

Start with one part, not the whole pile. Do the next piece at the speed you can keep for a month, not the speed you can keep for a day. One part at a walking rhythm, then stop. Setting things right doesn't need a season of effort; it needs one short motion made at a rhythm you'd still recognize next week.

cells.tense: You're the one who feels an imbalance first, and you keep it to yourself.
cells.act: state the order of things once, without argument
cells.ask: Say one imbalance between you and someone else out loud, once, then stop and give them room to reply.
cells.core:
You feel when something between people has gone out of proportion — that part is working. What's absent is your voice in it. The correction happens quietly, or it doesn't happen, and afterward you'd tell it as not being involved. Steering without saying you're steering reads as drift, and drift is expensive for the people living inside it.

Put the frame on the table before anyone asks: state the order of things once, without argument. One imbalance between you and someone else, said out loud, once, then stop and give them room to reply. You don't have to want the friction. The words themselves are the fair thing, and they hand someone else a turn.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the balance and tell it as if you're not there.
